MSK–SKIN · WEEK 17 · LECTURE 1

Anterior and Medial Thigh

Osteology · fascia · muscle action & innervation · femoral triangle & adductor canal · arteries and veins

Lecture Companion · Morganne Manuel, Ph.D. · 64-slide course source
ObjectivesOsteologyFasciaAnteriorMedialFemoral triangleAdductor canalNervesVesselsImagingMastery

Learning objectives & big picture

  1. Identify and describe clinically important hip and femoral bony landmarks, including those implicated in fractures.
  2. Relate anterior/medial thigh muscles to walking and running and predict consequences of injury.
  3. Explain thigh fascia and compartments, femoral sheath/canal/ring, catheterization, femoral hernias and lymphatic drainage.
  4. Trace arterial supply, venous return and the basis of varicose veins.
  5. Identify anterior/medial thigh structures on X-ray, MRI and CT images.

Big picture: Your hip and thigh move the limb forward, extend the knee, and draw the thigh toward the midline. Bone landmarks locate muscle attachments; fascial compartments organize these movements; the femoral triangle and adductor canal provide passage for large vessels and nerves. A disruption at one site can be predicted by the structures sharing that site.

MUST KNOW

Anterior compartment: hip flexion and knee extension, predominantly femoral nerve. Medial compartment: hip adduction, predominantly obturator nerve. Important exceptions are described below.

1 · Bony landmarks: build the three-dimensional map

The os coxae (innominate bone) forms from fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis, which all contribute to the cup-shaped acetabulum. The femoral head articulates with this socket. The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch, and the ligament of the femoral head carries an artery contributing to the femoral head’s blood supply.

Ilium: superior fan-shaped ala and iliac crest. The ASIS anchors sartorius and the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; the AIIS anchors rectus femoris. The inguinal ligament runs from ASIS to pubic tubercle, establishing the superior edge of the femoral triangle.

Ischium: ischial tuberosity, spine and ramus, obturator foramen, greater and lesser sciatic notches. Pubis: superior/inferior rami, pubic tubercle and pecten pubis; the inferior pubic ramus joins the ischial ramus as the ischiopubic ramus. See the lecture’s arcuate line and pecten pubis markings.

Femur: head, neck, shaft, greater and lesser trochanters, posterior intertrochanteric crest and linea aspera. Distally recognize medial/lateral condyles, epicondyles and the adductor tubercle. The tibial tuberosity receives the patellar ligament from the quadriceps extensor mechanism.

MUST KNOW

ASIS → sartorius; AIIS → rectus femoris; lesser trochanter → iliopsoas; adductor tubercle → hamstring part of adductor magnus; tibial tuberosity → patellar ligament.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why are the ASIS and AIIS not interchangeable?

Answer: Sartorius arises from the ASIS, while rectus femoris arises from the AIIS; these landmarks predict different hip and knee movements.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

The medial circumflex femoral artery provides a major pathway to the adult femoral head; disruption, especially around femoral neck injury, helps explain osteonecrosis. The lecture also explicitly addresses this arterial pathway later.

2 · Fascia lata and fascial compartments

The thigh is enclosed by fascia lata. Its lateral, medial and posterior intermuscular septa partition the thigh and channel the course of muscles and neurovascular structures. The thick lateral longitudinal band is the iliotibial tract, receiving fibers from gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae.

The key mental map is not simply a list of muscles: anterior = hip flexion / knee extension, medial = hip adduction, and posterior supplies important hip extensors and knee flexors. The lecture concentrates on the first two compartments.

COMMON CONFUSION

The iliotibial tract is a thickened portion of the fascia lata—not a separate thigh muscle. Its contributions come from gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae.

3 · Anterior thigh: muscle actions follow the attachments

The course organizes anterior thigh function around hip flexion and knee extension. The muscle’s path across a joint predicts its action: rectus femoris crosses hip and knee, so it both flexes the hip and extends the knee; the three vasti act principally at the knee.

MuscleProximal → distal attachment (lecture)InnervationAction / function
SartoriusASIS → medial tibia (pes anserinus)Femoral n.Flexes, abducts, laterally rotates hip; flexes knee
Rectus femorisAIIS and ilium → tibial tuberosity via quadriceps tendon/patellar ligamentFemoral n.Knee extension; assists hip flexion
Vastus lateralisGreater trochanter/linea aspera → tibial tuberosity via common extensor mechanismFemoral n.Knee extension
Vastus medialisIntertrochanteric line/linea aspera → tibial tuberosityFemoral n.Knee extension
Vastus intermediusAnterior/lateral femoral shaft → tibial tuberosityFemoral n.Knee extension
IliopsoasPsoas major: T12–L5 vertebrae/discs/transverse processes; iliacus: iliac crest/fossa → lesser trochanterPsoas: anterior rami; iliacus: femoral n.Powerful hip flexion

Why the quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament matter

Quadriceps heads converge on the quadriceps tendon, which attaches to the patella. Force continues through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Contracting the quadriceps therefore extends the knee through the patella rather than attaching directly to the tibia as an isolated muscle belly.

MUST KNOW

The four quadriceps heads are rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius. All are femoral-nerve supplied; all extend the knee; only rectus femoris also crosses the hip.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A femoral nerve injury weakens which especially testable movement?

Answer: Knee extension through the quadriceps, often with impaired hip flexion; the femoral nerve also supplies cutaneous branches.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Patellar tendon reflex primarily evaluates the L3–L4 segmental pathway through the femoral nerve. This is a useful clinical extension of the lecture’s quadriceps and femoral-nerve anatomy.

4 · Medial thigh: adductors, two-part magnus and pes anserinus

Medial compartment muscles pull the thigh toward the midline, providing control while walking and running. The lecture uses the obturator nerve as the general motor pattern, with the hamstring part of adductor magnus as an explicit exception.

MuscleProximal → distal attachmentInnervationPrincipal action
GracilisInferior pubic ramus → medial tibia (pes anserinus)Obturator n.Hip adduction; knee flexion; medial rotation of flexed leg
Adductor longusBody of pubis → linea asperaObturator n.Hip adduction
Adductor brevisInferior pubic ramus → pectineal line and linea asperaObturator n.Hip adduction
Adductor magnus — adductor partInferior pubic ramus → gluteal tuberosity/linea asperaObturator n.Hip adduction
Adductor magnus — hamstring partIschial tuberosity → adductor tubercleSciatic n. (lecture)Hip extension
Obturator externusExternal obturator membrane and adjacent rami → trochanteric fossaObturator n.Hip lateral rotation

Pes anserinus consists of three distal tendons attaching on the medial tibia: sartorius (anterior), gracilis (medial) and semitendinosus (posterior). The grouping links all three thigh compartments at one insertion site.

The adductor hiatus is an opening in the distal adductor magnus permitting the femoral artery and vein to reach the popliteal fossa; after the artery passes through, it is called the popliteal artery.

EXAM TRAP

Do not give all of adductor magnus one nerve or one action. Adductor part = obturator nerve/adduction; hamstring part = sciatic nerve/hip extension.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which adductor receives sciatic rather than obturator innervation?

Answer: The hamstring portion of adductor magnus, which extends the hip.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Pes anserine bursitis may present as focal pain over the anteromedial proximal tibia. The shared insertion explains why this location matters; bursitis itself was not taught in these slides.

5 · Femoral triangle, sheath, canal and femoral hernia

Read the femoral triangle like a topographic map: superior border = inguinal ligament; lateral border = sartorius; medial border = adductor longus. The floor is iliopsoas and pectineus; roof is fascia lata.

The lateral-to-medial organization is NAVEL: femoral Nerve, femoral Artery, femoral Vein, Empty space (femoral canal), Lymphatics. This order helps locate vessels for examination and catheterization.

The femoral sheath is a funnel-shaped fascial continuation passing deep to the inguinal ligament. It contains three compartments: lateral (artery), intermediate (vein), and medial (femoral canal with fat and lymphatics). Its proximal opening into the canal is the femoral ring. The femoral nerve is outside the sheath.

A femoral hernia passes abdominal contents through the femoral ring into the canal. The lecture notes greater frequency in females and highlights the ring’s narrow rigid boundaries, which can compress vessels supplying herniated bowel → ischemia and necrosis.

MUST KNOW

NAVEL is an order across the femoral triangle, not a list of four structures all enclosed by the sheath. The nerve sits lateral and outside the sheath; the canal is the medial sheath compartment.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

A femoral hernia typically presents below the inguinal ligament and is classically distinguished from an inguinal hernia by its relationship to the pubic tubercle. This adds a board-style surface-anatomy distinction to the lecture’s canal mechanism.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What separates the femoral artery and vein from the femoral nerve within the sheath?

Answer: The femoral nerve is not inside the sheath; artery, vein and femoral canal are the three enclosed compartments.

6 · Adductor canal and neurovascular pathway

The adductor canal runs from the inferior apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus. Lateral boundary: vastus medialis; medial/roof region: sartorius; posterior: adductor longus and magnus. Its named contents are femoral artery, femoral vein and saphenous nerve.

As you move distally, follow femoral triangle → adductor canal → adductor hiatus → popliteal fossa. The femoral vessels pass through the hiatus; the saphenous nerve is a cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, so it does not simply become the popliteal nerve or artery.

COMMON CONFUSION

The femoral canal and adductor canal are different. Femoral canal = medial compartment of femoral sheath containing fat/lymphatics; adductor canal = passage along mid/distal thigh for femoral vessels and saphenous nerve.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What changes name at the adductor hiatus?

Answer: Femoral artery becomes popliteal artery. The saphenous nerve travels in the adductor canal but is not renamed the popliteal nerve.

7 · Lumbar plexus and predicted sensory or motor deficits

The lumbar plexus is formed by anterior rami L1–L4 in the lecture. Major illustrated branches: femoral nerve (L2–L4), obturator nerve (L2–L4), lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh (L2–L3), and lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5).

NerveCourse / supply emphasized in slidesIf affected, predict
Femoral (L2–L4)Passes beneath inguinal ligament; supplies anterior-thigh muscles; anterior cutaneous branches and saphenous n.Weak knee extension; sensory change over anterior thigh and medial leg via relevant branches
Obturator (L2–L4)Passes through obturator canal; anterior and posterior branches to medial thigh (except hamstring magnus)Weak thigh adduction; medial-thigh sensory involvement
Lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–L3)Purely sensory; deep to inguinal ligament; supplies anterolateral thighAnterolateral sensory loss or paresthesias without weakness

The lecture’s lower-limb dermatome diagram places much of the anterior thigh in L2–L3. Dermatomes (spinal roots) and named peripheral-nerve cutaneous territories are not interchangeable maps.

MUST KNOW

Obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal (bony pelvis); femoral nerve passes deep to the inguinal ligament; lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Meralgia paresthetica is entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing burning/tingling over the anterolateral thigh WITHOUT motor loss. The source lecture establishes the purely sensory course; the syndrome name is added for Step 1.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Anterolateral thigh paresthesia but normal knee extension and hip adduction: which named nerve?

Answer: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3), a sensory-only branch.

8 · Arterial supply, venous return, and clinical applications

The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery on passing deep to the inguinal ligament. It enters the femoral triangle, travels through the adductor canal, and becomes the popliteal artery on traversing the adductor hiatus. Its major branch here is the deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery.

The profunda femoris gives rise to medial circumflex femoral (the lecture locates it between pectineus and iliopsoas) and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (deep to sartorius and rectus femoris), with ascending, transverse and descending lateral branches. The lecture associates loss of medial circumflex femoral supply with avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

The great saphenous vein begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, travels anterior to the medial malleolus then along the medial leg/thigh, and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening. With varicose veins, dilated veins and ineffective venous valve cusps permit backflow; the lecture notes that clots can form.

MUST KNOW

A single sequence links the routes: external iliac → femoral → popliteal artery, with the adductor hiatus marking the latter transition; great saphenous → femoral vein at the saphenous opening.

FIRST AID CONNECTION

Femoral neck fractures can threaten retinacular circulation from the medial circumflex femoral artery, leading to femoral-head osteonecrosis. This is closely aligned with the lecture’s AVN slide.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Where do you look for the great saphenous vein at the ankle?

Answer: Just anterior to the medial malleolus; it then ascends medially to meet the femoral vein at the saphenous opening.

9 · Imaging and unlabeled anatomy recognition

The stated learning objectives include identifying anterior/medial thigh structures on X-ray, MRI and CT. The provided 64-slide deck explicitly includes femoral-head X-ray examples in the avascular-necrosis slide, but does not include dedicated labeled thigh MRI/CT series. Use the lecture bone, compartment and vascular diagrams to establish what should be localized in cross-section; additional MRI/CT labeling is not claimed to be part of these slides.

For X-rays: find the femoral head, neck, greater/lesser trochanters, shaft, distal condyles and the acetabulum. On the AVN panel, compare preservation versus abnormality of the femoral head contour and density without assuming every feature can be seen equally in a small image.

For a transverse anatomy view: establish anterior/posterior orientation, find femoral shaft centrally, then identify vasti anterior/lateral, adductors medial/posterior, superficial fascia lata and canal neurovascular structures.

SOURCE LIMITATION

No dedicated CT or MRI thigh teaching images were present in the uploaded slide deck. This section teaches interpretation from the supplied anatomy diagrams rather than inventing an imaging demonstration.

Master these before moving on

  1. Attachment predicts action: ASIS vs AIIS, lesser trochanter, adductor tubercle, and tibial tuberosity locate the motor chain.
  2. Compartment predicts nerve: anterior/femoral versus medial/obturator, while iliopsoas components and adductor magnus hamstring portion are exceptions.
  3. NAVEL with a sheath caveat: femoral nerve is lateral and outside the femoral sheath; femoral canal is inside the sheath medial to the vein.
  4. Two different canals: femoral canal (hernia/lymphatics) versus adductor canal (vessels/saphenous nerve).
  5. Continuity of blood flow: external iliac → femoral → popliteal; profunda and medial circumflex connections explain femoral head AVN risk.

The most useful First Aid connections

  1. Patellar reflex: L3–L4 via femoral nerve.
  2. Femoral neck injury → impaired medial circumflex supply → osteonecrosis.
  3. Pure sensory lateral femoral cutaneous entrapment → meralgia paresthetica.
  4. Femoral versus inguinal hernias: location below versus above inguinal ligament (surface anatomy matters).
  5. Pes anserine bursa pain localizes to the shared medial tibial insertion.

FIRST AID CONNECTIONS are supplemental clinical/board associations, not statements that these syndrome names were presented in the slides.
